thought_path_snapshot: Identify the longest prefix of $s$ that matches $t$. This helps in determining the minimal part of $s$ that needs to be preserved to ensure $t$ remains a subsequence.

The previous approach incorrectly calculated the maximum removable substring by simply adding the lengths of the longest prefix and suffix matches of \( t \) in \( s \). This method fails when there are overlapping characters between the prefix and suffix matches, leading to an overestimation of the removable substring length.

The corrected strategy should focus on identifying the minimal contiguous segment in \( s \) that, when removed, still allows \( t \) to remain a subsequence. This involves finding the shortest interval in \( s \) that covers all characters of \( t \) in order, and then calculating the length of the substring outside this interval.
Identify the longest suffix of $s$ that matches $t$. Similar to the prefix, this helps in determining another minimal part of $s$ that needs to be preserved.

The previous approach incorrectly calculated the maximum length of the substring to remove by considering only the longest prefix and suffix matches separately. This method failed to account for the possibility of overlapping matches between the prefix and suffix of \( s \) that also match \( t \). The correct strategy should involve finding the longest contiguous segment in \( s \) that, when removed, still allows \( t \) to remain a subsequence of the remaining parts of \( s \). This requires a more nuanced approach to ensure that the removal does not disrupt the subsequence property of \( t \).

Use dynamic programming to create a table that records, for each position in $s$, the farthest position in $t$ that can be matched up to that point. This can help in identifying the maximum removable substring efficiently.
